newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong protesters demand China release dissidents.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong protesters demand China release dissidents.

text.p: Thousands of protesters took to the streets of Hong Kong on Sunday to demand that China release democracy activist Wang Dan and other jailed Chinese dissidents.
"Against political persecution of Wang Dan," demonstrators yelled as they marched to the headquarters of Xinhua news agency, Beijing's unofficial diplomatic mission here.

"Speech is innocent. Protest human rights," they chanted as they followed in the wake of two flatbed trucks decorated to resemble Chinese prison cells and transporting a quartet of protesters, hands chained and mouths taped shut to symbolise silencing of dissent in China.
Organisers said more than 3,000 protesters joined the noisy rally showing no concern they may attract China's anger in the countdown to the handover of the British colony next year.
Photographers and Reuters correspondents put the numbers of demonstrators brandishing banners and waving photographs of the 27-year-old Wang at between 2,000 and 3,000.

"Wang Dan has been sentenced to 11 years in prison. The same can happen to me or any other Chinese. Under this regime, our speech and thoughts can lead to such a harsh sentence," said exiled Chinese dissident Han Dongfang as he marched with his infant son on his shoulders.

Han is one of about 80 Chinese dissenters living in the colony facing an uncertain future when more than a century and a half of British rule ends next June 30 and the territory of six million people reverts to China.

Han was jailed for four years for taking part in the 1989 Tiananmen Square demonstrations in Beijing and fled to Hong Kong upon his release. The labour activist continues to agigate for better working conditions in China.
The sentencing of Wang, 27, on charges of conspiring to subvert the government points to a crackdown on dissent in Beijing and has unnerved the inhabitants of Hong Kong.
The colony was also shaken by remarks this month by Foreign Minister Qian Qichen suggesting that freedom of expression in Hong Kong would be limited after the handover.

A survey last week by a pro-Beijing business lobby group showed that most businessmen in Hong Kong expect less press freedom and see tighter controls on the political system and human rights after the handover.
Protests against China's crackdown on dissidents have become almost daily events in Hong Kong in recent weeks.
